planting.note: Set out divisions or small starts in spring once soil has warmed, in moist, humus-rich soil at the base of a trellis, fence, or shrub; the wiry twining stems need something to climb and spread quickly once established.

directions: Unlike most ferns grown for a mounded or arching clump, this species produces slender twining stems that climb by twisting around any available support, scrambling over fences, shrubs, and tree trunks in partial shade to light sun. Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil and provide a trellis or nearby planting for the thread-like fronds to grasp, since without support the stems simply tangle into a low mat. Cut the top growth back hard after hard frost blackens it; new stems resprout from the hardy rootstock each spring and can climb 6 to 10 feet in a single season under good conditions. This fern spreads readily by rhizome and wind-blown spores and has naturalized aggressively in parts of the warm, humid Southeast, so site it where its spread can be contained or monitored rather than near wild areas.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Divide and replant small sections of turf in cool spring weather into constantly damp, humus-rich soil or a wet rock-garden crevice; this alpine fern ally resents any summer drying and establishes best while temperatures are still mild.

directions: This diminutive, moss-like fern ally forms a low, bright-green mat of tiny scale-leaved stems that creep across constantly wet, cold, humus-rich ground in bogs, stream banks, and alpine turf. Unlike the tropical trailing spikemosses grown as houseplants, it is a true cold-hardy species native to northern and mountain regions, making it a candidate for a shaded rock garden, bog trough, or peat bed rather than a terrarium. Keep the soil saturated or constantly damp at all times, since this species has essentially no tolerance for drying out, and give it cool, dappled shade away from summer heat. It slowly knits together into a dense evergreen carpet and works well tucked among mossy stones or at the edge of a shaded water feature.

planting.note: Mount divisions with attached rhizome sections onto a slab, basket, or loose epiphytic mix in spring; new fronds root quickly from the furry creeping rhizomes once warm, humid growing conditions return.

directions: This Pacific Island epiphyte sends out thick, furry, pale rhizomes that creep visibly over bark, rock, or a hanging basket's edge, giving rise to the same furry-paw look as its better-known rabbit's-foot-fern relatives but with broader, more leathery, deeply divided fronds. Grow it mounted on a fern slab or in an open, fast-draining epiphytic mix in bright, filtered shade, letting the rhizomes ramble freely across the surface rather than burying them. Water and mist regularly through warm months to keep the humidity high, then let the mix dry slightly between waterings in cooler weather to avoid rot. Outside frost-free zones, grow it as a protected patio or greenhouse specimen and bring it indoors well before the first frost.

planting.note: Tuck small divisions into a shaded, lime-rich crevice or scree pocket in spring; this diminutive alpine fern needs sharp drainage around its roots even though the crown stays shaded and cool.

directions: Smaller and more finely cut than the common fragile fern, this European mountain species forms a tidy tuft of delicate, twice-divided fronds that emerge from limestone crevices and scree in its native alpine habitat. Plant it in a shaded trough, rock garden pocket, or wall crevice with gritty, fast-draining soil on the alkaline side, and keep roots cool even where the crown receives dappled light. It dies back to a resting crown in late summer heat or drought and resprouts with cooler, moister conditions, so avoid mistaking summer dormancy for plant loss. Because its deeply cut fronds are easily damaged by foot traffic or heavy mulch, site it where it can be left undisturbed among rocks.

planting.note: Divide offset pups with an intact shield frond in spring and mount on a slab or basket with a pad of sphagnum against the shield; this compact variety roots in and resumes active growth quickly once warm, humid conditions return.

directions: This naturally occurring, more compact variety of the common staghorn fern produces shorter, stiffer, more upright antler fronds than the typical pendulous bifurcatum, making it a better fit for smaller mounts, shelves, or hanging displays with limited drop. Mount it with its rounded, overlapping shield fronds held against a slab or basket of loose, fast-draining epiphytic mix, and position it in bright, filtered shade such as beneath a porch roof or high tree canopy. Water by soaking or thoroughly dunking the mount weekly in warm weather, letting it dry somewhat between waterings, and feed lightly during the growing season since it draws most nutrients from trapped leaf litter in habitat. It is frost-tender and must be moved under cover well before temperatures drop toward freezing.
